name: Cedar shoe inserts
lead: Cedar shoe inserts are wooden pieces, often shaped like shoe trees, placed in footwear between wearings. A shoe tree is described generally as a device placed in a shoe to preserve its shape.[2] In appearance and grooming communities they are discussed as a way to limit foot and shoe odour, since cedar is commonly said to absorb moisture and carry its own scent.

Foot odour is generally attributed to sweat combined with bacterial activity, and general references list foot hygiene, sock choice and medicated insoles among prevention measures.[1] No source consulted for this entry examines cedar specifically.
infobox: Shape retention, moisture and odour control

paras: Shoe trees are placed inside a shoe to help it keep its shape.[2] Cedar versions are among those sold to enthusiasts of leather footwear, and are marketed on the basis that the wood takes up moisture and has a natural aroma.

Sweat itself is odourless; odour arises when bacteria on the skin and in closed shoes break down sweat and dead skin, with species such as Brevibacteria and Staphylococcus epidermidis implicated.[1] Closed, padded shoes trap moisture, and general references recommend daily sock changes and keeping feet dry.[1]

lore.intro: Cedar inserts are mentioned as a low-cost odour-control and shoe-care measure in grooming discussion.

claims.claim: Cedar absorbs moisture and odour from shoes
claims.believers: Proponents say the wood dries shoes overnight and leaves a pleasant scent, reducing stale smell.
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing cedar inserts for foot or shoe odour; general references attribute odour to sweat and bacteria.[1]

card.summary: Wooden shoe trees said to soak up moisture and smell; popular in shoe care, with no trials on odour.
card.note: No studies on cedar for odour were found.

quick.overview:
Cedar inserts are wooden forms left in shoes between wears. They keep shape and are said to absorb moisture and add a woody scent.

In grooming circles they are used as a passive odour measure alongside sock and hygiene habits.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the porous wood draws moisture out of the shoe. Foot odour itself is attributed to bacteria acting on sweat.
quick.risks: No documented harms were found; no studies on odour effects were found either.
